name: A company builds three clients that call the same protected API through one identity provider: (1) an ASP.NET Core MVC portal rendered on the server, (2) a Blazor WebAssembly app for customers, (3) a nightly service that synchronises orders without any user. For each client choose the OAuth 2.0 grant type, say whether it is a confidential or a public client, and justify the choice. Then explain why you would not use the Resource Owner Password flow for the customer app.
answer:
(1) MVC portal: Authorization Code grant. It is a confidential client: it runs on the server and can keep a client secret. The user signs in at the identity provider (/connect/authorize), the code comes to the redirect_uri, and the server exchanges code + client ID + client secret at the token endpoint for an ID token and an access token.
(2) Blazor WebAssembly: Authorization Code with PKCE. It is a public client: its code runs in the browser, so a secret would not stay secret. The app creates a code verifier and a code challenge, sends the challenge to /authorize and the verifier with the code to the token endpoint; an intercepted code is useless without the verifier.
(3) Nightly service: Client Credentials. No user takes part; the service runs on a server (confidential) and authenticates with its client ID and client secret at the token endpoint, then calls the API with the access token.
Why not Resource Owner Password for (2): the app would collect the user's password itself and send it to the token endpoint – against the OAuth goal that users do not share credentials with applications; it also loses the identity provider's own login page (single sign-on, other login methods). The lecture recommends standards such as Authorization Code + PKCE instead.
keyPoints: MVC portal: Authorization Code, confidential client (secret kept on the server)
Blazor WebAssembly: Authorization Code with PKCE, public client (cannot keep a secret)
PKCE: challenge to /authorize, verifier to the token endpoint; intercepted code is useless
Nightly service: Client Credentials with client ID + secret, no user
Resource Owner Password exposes the user's password to the app, against delegated access
source: L7, slides 4, 6, 11-12, 27-31, 35; the loss of single sign-on and other login methods with the password flow is derived

name: A web shop keeps its own customer accounts. Requirements: customers register and sign in with e-mail and password; staff in the Admin group manage products; only customers whose stored birth date shows they are 18 or older may buy alcohol, and the check also needs the shop to be open for alcohol sales at that time; a customer who signs out on a shared computer must not stay usable through a stolen refresh token. Describe how you store passwords and what you avoid, how you express the authorization rules with roles, claims and policies, and how you handle refresh tokens.
answer:
Passwords: store only a one-way hash; at login hash the entered password and compare it with the stored hash. Do not use encoding (Base64 gives no security) and do not store passwords encrypted (they could be decrypted). Use an existing library such as ASP.NET Identity (or an external provider) – do not write your own crypto. No maximum password length; verify the e-mail address; support 2FA, but whether to force it depends on the audience.
Authorization: staff get the role Admin, and the product-management controller requires it. The birth date is a claim of the individual customer. The alcohol rule is a policy: a function that reads the birth-date claim, computes the age and checks the sales time, then grants or denies access; it is applied only to the checkout action that sells alcohol.
Refresh tokens: revoke the refresh token at logout (Duende does it by default; otherwise call /connect/revocation). Use refresh token rotation: every exchange returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one; with reuse detection an old token presented again invalidates the whole chain, so a stolen token stops working.
keyPoints: Passwords stored as one-way hashes and compared at login; no encoding or encryption
Use a library such as ASP.NET Identity, not own crypto; no maximum length, verify e-mail, optional 2FA
Admin group as a role on the product-management controller
Birth date as a user claim; the alcohol rule as a policy combining age and sales time
Refresh tokens revoked at logout or via /connect/revocation
Rotation with reuse detection invalidates a stolen refresh token chain
source: L7, slides 15, 17-24, 35; applying the policy only to the alcohol checkout action is derived
